title: Population History from One Genome
eyebrow: Lesson 4 · what one animal's genome says about its ancestors
intro: The two copies of every chromosome in one animal trace back to common ancestors that lived thousands to millions of generations ago, and how long ago they met depends on how large the population was. This lesson reads that record. It starts with the idea behind every method (the coalescent), then builds the input from one diploid genome, runs PSMC and reads its curve, turns model units into years and animals with a mutation rate and a generation time, and compares PSMC with MSMC2, SMC++, cobraa and methods that need many animals. Then come the checks that tell a real feature from an artefact, the two-species case (split time and gene flow with hPSMC, BPP and gIMble), and what a report must state so that others can judge and redraw the curve.

The running examples are two closely related rodents with one male genome each: our nanopore genome of a species called species A here, and the public HiFi assembly of a close relative ("the relative"). All their dates use placeholder rates, which is itself one of the lessons. Questions that need many animals (allele frequencies, recent history in detail, the standard gene-flow tests) are only outlined here; DNA methylation and an in-depth treatment of SINEs and satellites are left for later lessons. Hover over a dotted term to see what it means.
